Productive middle guide to arrival checks
New colleagues will find here what to practise
This page covers arrival checks for the Companion Animal Travel Desk and shows why the work matters. Every case moves through our desk with a live animal at stake, so careful checking protects welfare, keeps records clean, and helps crews act with confidence. Your task is to confirm what is booked, what is packed, and what must be shared before the animal reaches the aircraft or the destination desk.

Start with the booking file and read it as if you will need to explain it to another colleague. Match the traveler details, the animal details, and the route notes against the current record. Look for signs that the carrier, feed instructions, health papers, and handling notes all agree. If anything is unclear, stop and raise it at once rather than guessing. A small error at this stage can lead to delay, stress, or a missed handover.

At arrival, treat the animal and the accompanying paperwork as one set. Check that the crate is secure, ventilated, and suitable for the species and size. Confirm that labels are visible and that the live-animal status is easy to see. Then compare the handover notes with the latest crew message. The desk also shares practical instructions with crews, so your wording must be direct and consistent. Use plain language, avoid long explanations, and keep the focus on what the crew needs to do next.

When a traveler or escort arrives with concerns, stay calm and listen closely. Do not promise an outcome before you have checked the record. If the animal appears unwell, distressed, or mismatched with the paperwork, alert the senior coordinator and follow the escalation path without delay. If the case is routine, confirm the next step, file the arrival note, and pass the case forward in order.

Good desk work depends on repetition, accuracy, and steady communication. You are not only collecting forms; you are protecting a chain of care that begins at booking and ends at pickup. Remember to check every detail, speak clearly, and treat each animal handover as important.
